query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing the heavy element Hf in as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a lighter, similarly refractory element (Nb) will reduce the alloy density without compromising its mechanical performance at room temperature and at ~1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm3, exhibiting high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Substitute a portion of Hf with Nb (for example, designing an alloy with a mixed Hf/Nb sublattice such as Hf0.5Nb0.5MoTaTiZr), using the same vacuum arc melting process used for the as‐cast alloy.
generation.conditions: As‐cast microstructure; mechanical testing at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C under controlled loading conditions (e.g., tensile or compressive tests as previously used).
generation.structural_mediator: Sustained single-phase BCC structure and dislocation-based deformation mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Replacing Hf (atomic weight ~178.5) with the lighter Nb (atomic weight ~92.9) decreases the overall alloy density. Since Nb is also refractory and participates in solid solution strengthening, the substitution is expected to maintain or possibly enhance the high-temperature strength and ductility, provided that the alloy remains a stable single-phase solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a density reduction (potentially in the range of 5–10% lower than 10.21 g/cm3) while retaining similar yield strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C compared to the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with high strength and ductility at room temperature and ~1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from ambient to approximately 1000 °C; mechanical loading conditions as defined for standard tensile/compressive tests; valid for as‐cast microstructures synthesized via vacuum arc melting.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal substitution ratio (e.g., 50% Hf replacement) needs further tuning to ensure phase stability and uniform mechanical properties. There is uncertainty in whether the modified alloy may develop secondary phases if too much Hf is replaced.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the modified alloy (e.g., Hf0.5Nb0.5MoTaTiZr) using vacuum arc melting to obtain an as‐cast microstructure. Perform standardized tensile or compressive tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C. Compare the density, yield strength, and ductility against those of the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
measurements: Yield strength at room temperature and at ~1000 °C
Ductility (e.g., compressive/tensile strain) at both temperatures
Phase analysis (e.g., XRD) to confirm single-phase BCC structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substitution leads to a significant decrease in yield strength or ductility (beyond experimental variability) at room temperature or ~1000 °C, or if secondary phases form that compromise the alloy's microstructure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. chosen.lever: elemental substitution – partially replace the heavy refractory element (e.g., Hf) with a lighter but similarly refractory species such as Nb
chosen.technique: fabricate the new alloy via vacuum arc melting and perform standardized room‐temperature and high‐temperature (≈1000 °C) mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or compressive tests)
chosen.conditions: as‐cast condition; mechanical characterization at room temperature and at high temperature (≈1000 °C) under defined loading protocols
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the open niche by altering the alloy’s composition to reduce density while preserving mechanical performance. Prior evidence in high-entropy alloys indicates that substituting heavy refractory elements with lighter ones like Nb can maintain or even enhance high-temperature strength when the overall phase stability is retained. The proposed experimental plan – synthesizing the alloy and testing its mechanical properties – offers a straightforward method for falsifying the hypothesis if the yield or ultimate strengths fall significantly compared to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
